label: Claude Sonnet 5.5
output:
Here's a draft. I kept the patient deliberately vague and left the staffing complaints out entirely. Change anything that doesn't sound like you.

---

**The last night**

I did my last night shift on Saturday. 21:00 to 07:30, majors, a shift like any other except that I kept noticing things I wouldn't normally notice. Which trolley I was standing next to when the clock went past midnight. The sound the double doors make. How the corridor smells at 3am, which I won't try to describe except to say I'd know it blindfolded.

My first night was in 2012, when I was an SHO and thought I was far more capable than I was. This one was my last, at least for now. As of Monday I'm on the days-only rota. Fourteen years of nights, finished, and I am surprisingly not okay about it.

I've sat down to write this several times since spring, when I stopped updating this blog, and every attempt has turned into one of two things. Either a eulogy, which is ridiculous because nobody died, or a rant about the NHS, which you've all read before and which I've written enough of. So I'm going to try to just say what nights gave me and what they took, and see where that gets us.

**What they took**

The practical answer is my body, and I might as well admit it. My knees have opinions about the stairs. My sleep has been bad for a long time in a way that no amount of blackout curtains fixes. And my GP recently told me my blood pressure is not a joke anymore, in the tone of someone who has said it to a lot of doctors who then ignored her. So the move to days is partly sensible, partly overdue, and mostly something I'd have told any colleague to do.

The other thing they took is harder to put a number on. I missed both of my nieces' naming ceremonies, watching on video because I was either about to start a shift or had just come off one and couldn't be trusted to hold a conversation. My sister, who lives in Bangalore and has every right to be annoyed, never once complained. Not once. I'd like it on record that I noticed.

And in my first winter of nights, I cried in the car park at the Infirmary because I couldn't remember whether I'd given a second dose. I had. I checked, and I'd done it right, and I still sat there with the engine off and frost creeping up the windscreen, feeling like the least competent person in Leicestershire. I remember the frost better than I remember the patient. That's what the early nights did, they made everything very sharp and slightly unreal.

**What they gave**

People tend to think nights in emergency medicine are about adrenaline. Sometimes they are. But mostly nights are about staying kind at 5am when you are completely empty. Everyone's tired, the patients are frightened and the relatives have been in a plastic chair for six hours. You have nothing left, and you find out what you do with that.

What I learned is that the department is most itself at night. There are fewer managers, fewer meetings and fewer people performing being busy. There's more honesty, and a lot more kindness, and I don't think that's a coincidence. When you strip away the daytime machinery, what's left is a handful of people looking after each other and whoever comes through the door.

Last winter, at about 3am, an older man held my hand and told me I had his daughter's hands. I don't know why that landed the way it did. He was unwell and a bit confused, and he was probably just reaching for something familiar. But I stood there and let him hold on, because that was the job at that moment and nothing else on the board mattered more. He went home a few days later. I think about that more than I think about most of the cases that were technically harder.

Then there's Folasade, our charge nurse on nights. She has done nights for 22 years and she still beats me up the stairs. I've tried to catch her. I'm 42 and my knees are in open revolt, and she goes past me with a clipboard and no visible effort. She's taught me more about running a department than any course, mainly by example: you speak to the frightened person first, you don't raise your voice, and you do the small kind thing even when you think nobody will see.

And then there's the toast. Every night, at around 4am, someone makes toast in the staff room. Nobody admits to starting it. I've asked, and I've been lied to by people I'd trust with my life. The smell drifts down the corridor and within ten minutes half the shift has gathered, standing about with a slice each, not talking about anything much. It's the closest thing we have to a ritual and I've never once seen it organised.

**The relief**

Here's the part I'm least comfortable with. I'm relieved. I'm properly, physically relieved, in a way that has surprised me, and I feel like a traitor for it. I keep thinking that if nights meant as much as I say they did, I should be more reluctant to leave. But I think you can love something and be glad to put it down, and I'm trying to let both of those be true at once.

On Sunday morning I drove home down the London Road with the sun coming up and the shipping forecast on catch-up. I've done that drive more times than I could count, usually half asleep and fixated on getting to bed. That morning I was wide awake, and the light came in low and gold over the rooftops, and I thought: I won't see it from this side again. Not like this, not as the end of a shift. I turned the radio up a bit and listened to the sea areas all the way home.

**What's next**

I don't know yet what days will be like. I've been told they're different. More people, more noise, more of the things I used to be glad to miss. I expect I'll be bad at it for a while, the way you're bad at anything you've stopped being a beginner at for so long.

But I keep thinking about the staff room at 4am. Somewhere tonight, someone is going to put bread in the toaster, and nobody will admit to it, and by ten past a few tired people will be standing in a corridor eating toast. And Folasade will take the stairs two at a time and wait for the rest of them at the top.

It will carry on without me, and I find that's a comfort.

---

A few notes: it comes to about 1,100 words, so you have room to add if you want. I didn't say anything about how your first days went, since I don't know. If you'd like a line or two on that, it would probably fit just before "What's next."
